extracted.intended_audience: inventors and patent practitioners (lawyers, agents) seeking practical guidance on inventor attribution and recent case-law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for deciding who qualifies as the inventor (or joint inventor) for a letters patent and how assistance, prior use, and foreign communications affect patent validity and ownership. Focuses on attribution, servant/master issues, prior public use, and interpretation of specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of the inventor (no assistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: No person, who has not, without assistance, formed the original idea of the subject in his mind, will be enabled to keep any patent which he may have obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee must be the original inventor (i.e., have conceived the idea without assistance). The text emphasizes the necessity of independent origination; where assistance is present, other rules about employer/assistant apply (see Bloxam v. Elsee exception below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted assistance for completing mechanical means (Bloxam v. Elsee)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may be assisted by an engineer to complete the mechanical means for carrying his intentions into effect; additions made by that person will belong to the employer who may include them in the specification as part of his own invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the inventor must have the original idea, it is established (Bloxam v. Elsee) that skilled assistance employed expressly to complete mechanical contrivances does not defeat the employer's claim to the invention; the employer may incorporate the assistant's additions into the specification and claim them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master‑servant rule for improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the servant makes a new discovery by himself, such invention becomes his property; but if the master plans and the servant only executes with alterations, then the master is the true inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in cases such as Hill v. Thompson and illustrated by the Donkin/Foudriniers example: where a servant independently originates the invention, he owns it; where the servant was merely executing the master's plan (even with some alterations), the master is the inventor. Whether help is 'execution' or an independent discovery is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint patentees must each have contributed to the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-patent taken out in the joint names of two or three persons will be void if it is discovered that one or two of those persons bore no part in the invention of the machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing in joint names, ensure each named patentee actually contributed to the inventive conception; otherwise the patent can be invalidated for misattribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use must be a public use to defeat a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior use of a thing, by which an inventor will lose his patent if the subject has been used before, must be a public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees challenging novelty must show that prior use was public; mere private or partially concealed use may not bar a patent. Also patentees must be free from suspicion of having seen the prior machines in an imperfect or partially concealed state—being first to put into public use is not alone sufficient if there was prior inspection/knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small combinations of mechanical parts can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A very small combination of mechanical instruments may be the subject of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (Lewis v. Davis) supports that even modest mechanical combinations may qualify as patentable inventions; do not assume patentability requires large or complex assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts allow liberal construction of specification language
rubrics_metrics.description: Great latitude is allowed in constructing the meaning of the words used and the description of the invention given in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities such as Crosley v. Beverley, Lewis v. Marling, and Jones v. Pearce show courts will interpret specification language liberally to give effect to the inventor's intentions; drafters should nonetheless aim for clarity, but may rely on courts' willingness to construe wording broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introducer of a foreign invention and alien‑interest issue
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention has been obtained from a foreigner, it is common practice to state in the title that the patentee received the communication from a person residing abroad; it has been doubted whether the patent can be supported if the foreign inventor, retaining any interest in the patent, is an alien enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating the foreign source is optional; however, caution is warranted if the foreign originator retains an interest and is an 'alien enemy'—this may raise enforceability issues. Conversely, a communication from a foreign resident to a domestic recipient will usually allow the domestic recipient to be treated as the first inventor for patent purposes.
